newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan people dissatisfied, pessimistic - poll.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan people dissatisfied, pessimistic - poll.

text.p: People in Taiwan are increasingly dissatisified with their lives and becoming more pessimistic over their future, according to a newspaper poll published on Thursday.

The survey, conducted by the mass-circulation United Daily News, showed that 62 percent of 1,168 respondents said they were "satisfied" with their current lives, compared to 69 percent in 1995 and a high of 77 percent in 1993.

Only 28 percent said most people in Taiwan would live better three years from now, while 32 percent predicted most would be worse off -- the first time that pessimists have outnumbered optimists since the paper launched the annual poll in 1987.
The daily attributed the malaise to a lack of confidence in the economy, which has slowed from its "Asian dragon" days of double-digit growth in the 1980s.

An overwhelming 87 percent felt the economy has been mired in a slump in 1996, up from 82 percent in 1995 and a low of 46 percent in 1994. Only seven percent thought the economy was in a satistactory state.
Taiwan's government has predicted full-year 1996 gross domestic product growth (GDP) of just 5.7 percent, which would mark the island's slowest growth rate since 1990.
GDP growth has defied state efforts to engineer a significant recovery.
The survey, whose questionnaire has been the same since 1987, did not ask specifically how the long shadow of Taiwan's huge rival China affected the local quality of life.

Taiwan and the Chinese mainland have been divided since the end of a civil war in 1949 and Beijing has stepped up pressure in recent years to bring the Nationalist-ruled island under the communist mainland's sovereignty.

Analysts say China's influence is seen chiefly in the performance of Taiwan's economy, which is highly dependent on Hong Kong, which will revert to Chinese rule in 1997, and increasingly reliant on the mainland economy itself.

Experts have blamed Taiwan's economic slowdown in part on political tensions with China, which peaked in March 1996 as Beijing mounted dramatic war games that it acknowledged were a bid to frighten Taiwan voters out of any hopes of independence.
Other factors contributing to the slowdown include poor domestic investment and a prolonged slump in Taiwan's real estate industry.
